Metadata verified against the Columbia University Press catalogue page, the PhilPapers record, and the Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews notice (review by Joerg Tuske). The volume collects work by the principal living apoha scholars and pairs the philological chapters with a second half that tests exclusion semantics against contemporary cognitive science. The book itself has not yet been acquired; all wording carried below is verified against secondary surfaces (SEP, NDPR, publisher copy) and awaits collation against the printed pages. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Mark Siderits, Tom Tillemans, and Arindam Chakrabarti, eds., *Apoha: Buddhist Nominalism and Human Cognition* (New York: Columbia University Press, 2011). **Shortened note:** Siderits, Tillemans, and Chakrabarti, *Apoha*. **Bibliography:** Siderits, Mark, Tom Tillemans, and Arindam Chakrabarti, eds. *Apoha: Buddhist Nominalism and Human Cognition*. New York: Columbia University Press, 2011. ## Source scholarship Dignāga's doctrine of *anyāpoha* ("exclusion of the other"), set out in chapter 5 of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, answers a nominalist's problem: if there are no real universals, what does a general term hook onto? Dignāga's answer is that a word refers not by grasping a shared positive essence but by excluding everything the word does not apply to. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's Dharmakīrti entry (Tillemans, rev. 2026) transmits Dignāga's own formulation from the *Sāmānyaparīkṣā*: "A word talks about entities only as they are qualified by the negation of other things." "Cow" reaches every cow by carving away the non-cows; the extension is delivered by the cut, not by a resemblance the cuts merely trace. The load-bearing subtlety — the one the essay's whole use of apoha depends on — is that the double negation does not collapse. "Pot" refers to every individual that is not a non-pot, and this is not a laborious way of saying "pot refers to pots." Tuske's NDPR review flags the distinction the volume's contributors work hardest on: the difference between nominally bound and verbally bound negation. A verbally bound negation ("it is not the case that x is a non-pot") would cancel out classically; the nominally bound negation of apoha instead forms a term whose content just is the exclusion, so "not non-p" retains a structure that plain "p" lacks. The negative detour is constitutive, not eliminable — the exclusion is remembered in the reference it achieves. This is exactly the feature the essay needs held open, and it is scholarship's own distinction, not the essay's imposition. Dharmakīrti's development then converts semantic exclusion into what the SEP entry calls "a type of causal theory of reference" (SEP §2.2.2): terms are grounded in the causal capacities of particulars to produce shared judgments and satisfy shared purposes, so that exclusion classes track causal-functional kinds without positing universals. This is the natural bridgehead toward training-signal readings of reference, and the volume's second half — chapters testing apoha against error-driven learning, concept formation, and cognitive science generally — shows the scholarly community itself already walking partway across that bridge, though never as far as modern machine-learning architectures. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution The volume is the essay's canonical carrier for apoha scholarship: Dignāga's exclusion semantics, the nominally/verbally bound negation distinction that keeps "not non-p" from reducing to "p", and Dharmakīrti's causal turn. ### Licensed essay use - Establish, on scholarly authority, that in apoha a word's positive reach is achieved through a negation that does not cancel — exclusion is constitutive of reference. - Carry the Dignāga formulation (via SEP) and the not-non-pot formulation as the textual basis for the essay's reading of apoha in [[10-s0-p3-apoha]]. - License the Dharmakīrti causal-theory step as the scholarly platform from which the essay's own softmax/argmax bridge departs in [[38-s5-p1-apoha-softmax]]. ### Claim boundary The volume carries apoha scholarship and nothing more. The softmax/argmax bridge and the formulation "exclusion that remembers" are the essay's own moves, registered as Argued/Offered with the novelty qualifier "to our knowledge": searches this cycle found no peer-reviewed work connecting apoha to machine-learning normalization; the nearest object is an unrefereed 2026 preprint by Subhash Kak, deliberately not admitted as a source. A. R. Price (Cambridge: Polity, 2017), 80–81. **Shortened note:** Lacan, *Talking to Brick Walls*, 80–81. **Bibliography:** Lacan, Jacques. *Talking to Brick Walls: A Series of Presentations in the Chapel at Sainte-Anne Hospital*. Translated by A. R. Price. Cambridge: Polity, 2017. ## Recoverability and verification The selected English carrier is the 2017 Polity translation, ISBN 9780745682426. The French parent edition is Jacques Lacan, *Je parle aux murs: Entretiens de la chapelle de Sainte-Anne* (Paris: Éditions du Seuil, 2011), ISBN 9782020971669. Seuil’s publisher record, the GHU Paris psychiatric-library catalogue, and ETH Zürich’s contents PDF verify the French object, its three Sainte-Anne presentations, and the 6 January 1972 “Je parle aux murs” presentation. No lawful local copy was present in the Books pool on 2026-07-14. The two short English passages in [Quotes — Lacan Talking to Brick Walls (Price, 2017)](#passages) were manually transcribed from Daniel Adleman and Chris Vanderwees’s open, university-hosted scholarly article, which identifies the Price translation and pp. 80–81. They are **source-matched**, not quotation-ready, until a page image or ePub of the authorised Polity/Seuil edition has been inspected directly. ## Essay use This primary source supplies the concrete scene of address to walls: a speaking that is not reducible to a failed lecture or a self-contained monologue. It is the correct primary carrier for the local phenomenology/rhetoric of the wall in movement 34. **Claim boundary:** this source does not say that `S/s = X/x`, that the wall is a Jungian general/particular relation, that a matheme resolves the wall, or that Lacan anticipated QL’s crossed-zero and `0/1` sequence. Darmon’s `S/s` genealogy and the essay’s `X/x` correspondence remain distinct: their relation is an **Argued** QL crosswalk. ## Passage preparation Exact text, source-match status, and consumer mappings: [Quotes — Lacan Talking to Brick Walls (Price, 2017)](#passages). ## Passages and excerpts ### Material metadata - **Edition consulted:** Jacques Lacan, Talking to Brick Walls: A Series of Presentations in the Chapel at Sainte-Anne Hospital, trans. A. R. Price (Cambridge: Polity, 2017). - **Access provenance:** Recoverable publisher edition; exact short passages manually transcribed from their lawful reproduction in Adleman and Vanderwees, English Studies in Canada 47, nos. 2–3 (2021), p. 222; direct authorised-edition page collation pending. ## Passage card — `lacan-2017-talking-to-brick-walls-q001` — Chapel as brick-wall address > “How is one to know to whom I am speaking? … I’m speaking to the chapel, that is, to the brick walls. This bungled action is becoming increasingly successful. Now I know to whom I’ve come to talk, to the very same I’ve always talked to at Sainte-Anne—to the brick walls … I’ve always been talking to the brick walls here.” - **Locator:** A. R. Price trans., *Talking to Brick Walls* (Polity, 2017), p. 80; “Talking to Brick Walls,” third Sainte-Anne presentation, 6 January 1972. - **Context:** Having been moved from the Magnan amphitheatre into the chapel, Lacan turns that displacement into the “bungled action” of discovering whom he has always addressed at Sainte-Anne. - **Status:** source-matched. - **Verification:** coordinator, 2026-07-14; manually transcribed from the typeset quotation in Daniel Adleman and Chris Vanderwees, “Lacan’s Psychoanalytic Rhetoric and the Power of Non-Understanding,” *English Studies in Canada* 47, nos. 2–3 (2021): 222, which identifies the Price translation and p. 80; no OCR; direct authorised-edition collation pending. - **Source relation:** extracted, pending direct-edition collation. - **Evidential action:** contextualises. - **Argument function:** authorial provenance / qualification of address and transmission. - **Consumers:** [[34-s4-p3-lacan-matheme-mytheme]]; [[Immutable Gap and Meta-Sign]]; [[Arche-Topos as Differential Field]]; movement 34’s `S/s ↔ X/x` argued crosswalk. - **Use boundary:** establishes Lacan’s brick-wall address in this presentation; it does not establish `S/s = X/x`, a Jungian reading of the wall, a doctrine of the matheme, or any QL relation. ## Passage card — `lacan-2017-talking-to-brick-walls-q002` — Voice as reverberation rather than direct transmission > “one has to tune one’s voice to the reverberation off the walls” - **Locator:** A. R. Price trans., *Talking to Brick Walls* (Polity, 2017), p. 86. - **Context:** The presentation turns from the displaced chapel scene to how address returns through a wall; Adleman and Vanderwees set this beside analyst and analysand listening together for what a sealed monologue has not yet made available. - **Status:** source-matched. - **Verification:** coordinator, 2026-07-14; manually transcribed from the typeset quotation in Adleman and Vanderwees, 222; no OCR; direct authorised-edition collation pending. - **Source relation:** extracted, pending direct-edition collation. - **Evidential action:** supports. - **Argument function:** primary rhetorical mechanism for mediated address. - **Consumers:** [[34-s4-p3-lacan-matheme-mytheme]]; [[Immutable Gap and Meta-Sign]]; movement 34’s transmission problem. - **Use boundary:** establishes a local image of echo and tuning; it does not state a doctrine of `S/s`, a matheme, or QL’s general/particular relation. ## Passage card — `lacan-2017-talking-to-brick-walls-q003` — Discourse remains bound to its wall > “is bound to the walls by a definition of discourse” - **Locator:** A. R. Price trans., *Talking to Brick Walls* (Polity, 2017), p. 100. - **Context:** The line is cited by Adleman and Vanderwees when they draw a limit on analytic authority: discourse and its theoretical scaffolding carry their own obstructions. - **Status:** source-matched. - **Verification:** coordinator, 2026-07-14; manually transcribed from the typeset quotation in Adleman and Vanderwees, 224; no OCR; direct authorised-edition collation pending. - **Source relation:** extracted, pending direct-edition collation. - **Evidential action:** qualifies. - **Argument function:** limitation on a totalising or transparent reading of formalisation. - **Consumers:** [[34-s4-p3-lacan-matheme-mytheme]]; [[Immutable Gap and Meta-Sign]]; movement 34’s non-closure condition. - **Use boundary:** establishes a stated limit internal to discourse; it does not identify the wall with QL’s bar or establish that a matheme escapes its own condition. ## Passage card — `lacan-2017-talking-to-brick-walls-q004` — The audience remains inside the address > “Talking to brick walls does indeed concern a few people.” - **Locator:** A. One institutional witness reports p. 30, so the authorised page must resolve this edition/locator conflict before promotion. - **Context:** This occurs in the earlier presentation of the same Sainte-Anne sequence, not in the 6 January brick-wall scene. Before final citation, record the page's displayed title/revision date and stable media identifier; use transcript paragraph/time locators rather than inventing pagination. ## Essay use Primary dialogue for observer/observed, truth/reality, and Bohm's recollection of a spinning wheel with a “thread running straight.” The image supports the complex-plane/artistic discussion of a movement that runs true through transformation. **Passages needed:** exact context of the wheel/thread image; observer/observed; truth and reality; limits of thought. **Claim boundary:** the complex modulus/thread alignment is the essay's mathematical interpretation.
